chapters.title: Chapter 2: Building Blocks: Randomness, Volatility, and Brownian Motion

lessons.title: Geometric Brownian Motion and the Lognormal Assumption

children.text: Fixing the Random Walk: Percentage Steps, Not Rupee Steps

The last lesson's coin-flip walk had a fixable flaw: fixed rupee steps that ignore price level and can, with enough bad luck, push a price below zero. The fix is to flip a coin for a percentage move instead of a rupee move. Heads means multiply the price by 1 plus some percentage; tails means multiply by 1 minus that percentage. A product of positive numbers is always positive, so this single change makes a below-zero price mathematically impossible, no matter how unlucky the sequence of flips gets.
A Surprising Twist: Equal Moves Don't Cancel

Rerun the exact same 10-flip sequence from the last lesson, heads-tails-heads-heads-tails-tails-tails-heads-heads-tails, but now each heads multiplies Nifty by 1.005 (up 0.5%) and each tails multiplies it by 0.995 (down 0.5%), instead of adding or subtracting a flat 50 points.

body.caption: The same 10-day sequence, now with percentage steps

body.label: Volatility drag, in one number
body.context: Five up moves and five down moves of the identical 0.5% size still leave Nifty slightly below where it started. This is not rounding error. For any x, (1 + x)(1 − x) = 1 − x², which is always a little less than 1. Pairing an up move with an equal-sized down move always leaves you a touch poorer, and the effect compounds every time it happens.

body.title: Feel the drag yourself
body.prompt: A stock starts at ₹1,000. It rises 2% one day, then falls 2% the next. What is the closing price after both moves?
body.explanation: ₹1,000 × 1.02 × 0.98 = ₹999.60. A 2% gain followed by a 2% loss does not return you to ₹1,000. It leaves you 0.04% (2% squared) short, exactly as (1 + x)(1 − x) = 1 − x² predicts.

children.text: From Percentage Steps to Geometric Brownian Motion
Shrink each step from one full day down to an instant, and let there be infinitely many of them between now and expiry. Percentage steps taken to this continuous-time limit are called
, or GBM, and it is the specific process Black-Scholes assumes every underlying follows.

markDefs.definition: A random process where the percentage change over an infinitesimally small time step is normally distributed, making the process itself always positive and its future value lognormally distributed.

body.caption: In words: the percentage change in price over a tiny instant (dS/S) equals a steady drift (μ dt) plus a random shock (σ dW) sized by volatility σ. This is the continuous-time version of the percentage coin flip you just ran by hand.

children.text: Solve that equation forward to any future date T, and the price at that date works out to the formula below. Look closely at the second term inside the brackets. That minus-a-half-sigma-squared is not decoration. It is the exact same volatility drag you just calculated by hand with the coin flips, now baked directly into the model as the price of accepting randomness at all.

body.caption: S₀ is today's price, μ is the drift, σ is volatility, T is time in years, and Z is a single draw from the standard normal distribution. Chapter 3 reuses this exact formula to build risk-neutral option pricing.

columns.label: Simple additive random walk
points: Fixed rupee-sized steps, same for any price level
Can push the price below zero
Price at any future date is normally distributed
Equal up and down moves exactly cancel out

columns.label: Geometric Brownian motion
points: Percentage-sized steps that scale with the current price
Price can never go below zero
Price at any future date is lognormally distributed
Equal-magnitude percentage up and down moves leave a small net loss, the volatility drag

body.title: Illustrative shape: where Nifty might land in one month

children.text: Over a single month this illustrative spread looks close to symmetric, and it roughly is at short horizons and ordinary volatility levels. The asymmetry is structural, not optional: the left side is hard-bounded, Nifty cannot fall below zero no matter how bad the month, while the right side has no ceiling at all. Stretch the same logic out to a year, or apply it to a far more volatile stock, and the right-hand tail visibly stretches out longer than the left. That built-in one-sided ceiling on downside and open-ended upside is a direct consequence of modeling price changes multiplicatively.

body.title: Why switch to percentage steps at all
body.question: What does switching from fixed rupee steps to fixed percentage steps guarantee about the modeled price?
options: The price can never exceed its starting value
The price can never fall to zero or below, since it is a product of positive factors
Every daily move is always positive
The expected return becomes exactly zero
body.explanation: Multiplying a positive price by positive factors, whether each factor is above or below 1, always produces another positive number. This is the specific property the additive random walk from Lesson 2.1 was missing.

body.text: Prices cannot be negative, so the model of how they move cannot be additive. Switching to percentage steps fixes that, but it also quietly changes the shape of the future: the price distribution stops being a symmetric bell curve and becomes lognormal, bounded on one side and open-ended on the other.

points: Replacing fixed rupee steps with fixed percentage steps guarantees the modeled price always stays positive.
Equal-magnitude percentage up and down moves do not cancel out. (1 + x)(1 − x) = 1 − x², so pairing them always leaves a small net loss called volatility drag.
Geometric Brownian motion (dS/S = μ dt + σ dW) is percentage-step randomness taken to a continuous-time limit, and it is the process Black-Scholes assumes every underlying follows.
Solving that equation shows the future price is lognormally distributed, with a −σ²/2 drift correction that is exactly the volatility drag effect, now built into the formula.
Lognormal prices are hard-bounded at zero on the downside but open-ended on the upside, unlike the symmetric normal distribution an additive walk would produce.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The Nifty levels, percentage steps, and the illustrative distribution chart are hypothetical, built to explain geometric Brownian motion, not to forecast actual index levels.
